Beállítom A szabadság koalícióját, a szabadság köreit kell megalkotnia a Fidesz politikai közösségének – erről beszélt Bóka János a kötcsei piknik előtt tartott sajtótájékoztatón. A Fidesz frakcióvezetője szerint a Fidesz ma egyszerre politikai ellenzéke a kormánynak és annak a rendszernek, amit a Tisza-kormány az önkényre épít. A kötcsei találkozóról azt mondta, az a szépsége, hogy itt nem pártpolitikai kérdésekről van szó, mindig nyitott eszmecsere, vita, párbeszéd zajlik. Szerinte Orbán Viktor folytatni fogja a politizálást, véget ért a nyári szabadsága, és felvette a munka fonalát. Bóka a Telex kérdésére elmondta: Orbán elkötelezettsége az ország és a politikai közösség iránt vitathatatlan. Egy másik válaszban egyértelművé tette, hogy a politikai közösség megkérdőjelezhetetlen vezetője még mindig Orbán. Szűcs Gábor fideszes képviselő is ott volt Bóka mellett a sajtótájékoztatón. Többször is említette: a Tisza-kormány cserben hagyta az autósokat azzal, hogy csak a dízelesek kapnak támogatást az államtól. „Az autósok háromnegyede nem fog ebből kapni, a fuvarozók közül 0 százalék” – mondta Szűcs, aki Bókával együtt idézte fel, hogy az előző kormány alatt mindenkire vonatkozott a védett árak rendszere, mindenki olcsóbban tankolhatott. Fotó: Hevesi-Szabó Lujza / Telex Legutóbb 2009-ben ment neki ellenzékből a Fidesz a párt körüli holdudvar egyik legfontosabb éves rendezvényének, az őszi politikai szezont 2004 óta megnyitó kötcsei pikniknek. Akkor viszont teljesen más volt a helyzet: a Fidesz jó esélyekkel állt egy közelgő választás előtt, most azonban egyre romló támogatottságot mutatnak az elbukott választás utáni közvélemény-kutatások. Az egyébként mindig zárt ajtók mögött tartott találkozó 2025-ben nem volt teljesen exkluzív . Orbán Viktor beszédét élőben lehetett követni, itt jelentette be Orbán a győzelmi tervüket a választásra, amely aztán annyira nem jött be a Fidesznek, hogy a Tisza kétharmaddal nyert. Illustration: Guardian Design Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza Harry Davies and Yuval Abraham Mon 16 Nov 2026 06.00 EST Last modified on Mon 16 Nov 2026 09.05 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Israel has in recent years migrated huge volumes of data into Amazon’s datacentres. Illustration: Guardian Design The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal. Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza. The images were uploaded by a department of the Israeli military that holds a vast collection of photos covering the Palestinian populations in Gaza and the West Bank . The department informed Amazon of the decision to upload the images in early 2024 so it could use Rekognition, the company’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project. The documents obtained by the Guardian form part of an investigation into the Israeli military’s reliance on the technology and infrastructure of Amazon’s cloud computing business to monitor Palestinians. According to the files and interviews with military sources, Israel has in recent years migrated huge volumes of data – including sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation – into Amazon’s datacentres. The large set of images was moved into an Amazon datacentre near Tel Aviv by a department commonly known as Rolling Stone, which sits within a military software unit. View image in fullscreen Displaced Palestinians wait to cross a checkpoint in Mughraqa in central Gaza in January 2025. Photograph: Eyad Baba/AFP/Getty Images The department takes its name from a system widely used by the Israeli military that serves as a central repository of information about Palestinians living in Gaza and the West Bank. At the time, the department was exploring using facial recognition technologies to analyse the extensive catalogues of images of Palestinians it holds, several sources with knowledge of its work said. After Israel’s ground invasion of Gaza in October 2023, its military routinely collected images of Palestinians as they passed through checkpoints, often after they had been forcibly displaced by the bombing campaign. It’s not clear whether the 3.5m images uploaded to Amazon’s Rekognition were captured at these checkpoints, which effectively served as pop-up surveillance posts. However, a military source familiar with facial recognition efforts at the checkpoints said Amazon’s cloud infrastructure was used due to the “very large scale” of images collected at the sites. Israel has long used facial recognition technology, particularly in its occupation of the West Bank. Face scanning is routine at checkpoints, while Israeli soldiers use custom-built smartphone apps to collect images of people living in the Palestinian territory. In the early stages of its campaign in Gaza, Israel used Rekognition to identify hostages captured by militants in the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. The military also deployed facial recognition technology to identify people it suspected were militants. The New York Times has previously reported how the military experimented with commercially available technology in Gaza to detect faces in crowds and in drone footage, at times wrongly flagging civilians as militants. The new documents reveal the Israeli military’s use of Amazon technology, both for experiments with facial recognition and for a more far-reaching project to move its data on to the servers of the computing arm of the conglomerate founded by billionaire Jeff Bezos . View image in fullscreen Amazon founder Jeff Bezos speaks at the America Business Forum in Miami last year. Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/AP They also shed light on what the Israeli military is moving into the cloud and how it uses Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure to support the collection and processing of Palestinians’ personal data, typically gathered indiscriminately, through intrusive means and without their consent. The files suggest the ties between AWS and the Israeli military deepened during a period in which Israel has been accused of committing grave crimes in Gaza, including genocide – a charge denied by Israel, but supported by a UN commission of inquiry, Israeli human rights groups and genocide experts. A spokesperson for AWS said it had no “visibility” into workloads held by its customers in its cloud. They added: “We respect the privacy of our customers, and we do not discuss our relationship without their consent.” An embrace of big tech In early 2024, a small group of Israeli soldiers worked from AWS’s offices in Tel Aviv, located on the 28th floor of one of Israel’s tallest skyscrapers. The soldiers were exploring ways to use the company’s cloud infrastructure to more effectively operate a facial recognition programme underway in Gaza, several military sources said. It’s not clear whether their work was made operational or if it related to the 3.5m images uploaded to Rekognition. The presence of the group at AWS’s offices, however, underscores the close relationship between the Israeli military and the cloud provider. An AWS spokesperson said its customers “regularly visit our offices for briefings and meetings”. They added: “Any suggestion that these visits are anything other than routine customer engagement is wrong and unsubstantiated.” The foundation of Israel’s relationship with Amazon is a sweeping 2021 contract known as Project Nimbus. Under the multibillion dollar deal, AWS and Google provide cloud services to a wide range of government and military clients. The Guardian revealed last year that the Nimbus contract contains unusual terms that prohibit the US companies from restricting or suspending Israeli government and military use of their cloud services, even if Israel breaches their terms of service. This would prevent the kind of unilateral action taken by Microsoft last year when it disabled the Israeli military’s access to technology used to operate a mass surveillance system uncovered by the Guardian and +972 Magazine . View image in fullscreen A surveillance camera is pictured at a checkpoint in the Palestinian city of Hebron in 2021. Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty Images As part of the Nimbus deal, AWS opened new datacentres in Israel in early 2023, allowing the Israeli government and military clients to migrate data from their own servers, according to documents. A large proportion of data was also moved from AWS datacentres in Ireland. A central component of the Nimbus contract, files show, was an obligation on AWS to provide the Israeli military with access to a segregated area within its Tel Aviv datacentres, fortified with enhanced digital and physical security measures. This isolated area within the AWS cloud – used to store sensitive material relating to military operations and intelligence collection – was described by the company and its client as a “walled garden”. The Israeli military’s reliance on AWS reflects its embrace in recent years of leading US tech companies to meet the technological demands of war with rapidly scalable storage, computing power and AI-driven services. The role of AI in Israel’s offensive in Gaza has come under fresh scrutiny particularly after the release of NAZA , a Guardian-produced documentary about the remote surveillance and killing of Palestinian civilians. ‘The plan was to migrate everything’ The Rolling Stone department is among AWS’s most significant Israeli military clients, documents suggest. Its use of Rekognition in early 2024 to analyse 3.5m images came after it had expanded its use of AWS products and services to store and analyse its data. Files show the department migrated significant volumes of the data it holds into the so-called “walled garden” in AWS’s cloud throughout 2023. A military source involved in this effort said it had planned to move all of its databases from the military servers into AWS’s cloud. The source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said: “The plan [at Rolling Stone] was to migrate pictures, videos, all the confidential intelligence information – everything.” A spokesperson for the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it “does not intend to comment on engagements or services related to operational needs”. The Rolling Stone department oversees several expansive databases that collate data on Palestinians, including the system from which the branch takes its name. Used by the military for decades, the Rolling Stone system is constantly updated and includes data such as basic personal and family details, property holdings, and information on checkpoint crossings, work permits, and criminal activity. A soldier who provided testimony to Breaking the Silence, an Israeli NGO, in 2016 described Rolling Stone as “a computerised system where all the information relevant to the control of the Palestinian civilian population is centralised”. As a result of Israel’s control of the population registries covering Gaza and the West Bank, the Rolling Stone department has amassed millions of Palestinians’ photographs taken for the identity cards issued to every resident when they turn 16 years old. Sources familiar with its work said the images were routinely used for facial recognition programmes. These include Blue Wolf, a smartphone app Israeli soldiers use in the West Bank to scan Palestinians’ faces and access information about them, including whether they’ve been flagged as suspects for arrest. In Gaza, at temporary Israeli checkpoints established after the ground invasion, cameras trained on Palestinian people were used to capture their images as they approached the sites. Facial recognition was then used to match people to images held in Rolling Stone’s systems, sources said. The checkpoints became notorious in Gaza as places where people were pulled aside and detained. Many were taken into Israeli custody and held incommunicado, amounting to enforced disappearances, according to several UN bodies and rights groups. Documents suggest AWS’s cloud technology was used at times during 2024 to support the work of the checkpoints. Military insiders said the checkpoints were referred to by Israeli soldiers as Nakaz – a Hebrew word for drainage. Harry Davies is one of the Guardian producers on NAZA, which Yuval Abraham co-directed. NAZA is now in cinemas worldwide and will screen for free on the Guardian’s website from early December.
